Additionally, we derive the corresponding formula for the chromatic cone curvature and examine the feasibility of a chromatic 2-space being described as a hypersurface.

The selection of an appropriate loss function is a critical factor in developing a deep neural network classifier. Although the standard approach is to use the mean squared error loss function, researchers have been exploring alternative options, including the zero-one loss function. However, the underlying mechanism of the zero-one loss function remains unclear due to its non-differentiable nature. In an effort to address this issue, two novel loss functions have been proposed in this paper, the novel circumjacent 01 loss function and the circumjacent 01 loss function with exponential decay, both of which are designed to imitate the zero-one loss function's behavior. By conducting a series of experiments, the influence of using the zero-one loss function was assessed, and the proposed loss functions were compared to the standard mean squared error loss function. Furthermore, a step-by-step guide on how to use the proposed functions was also shared in this paper.

This study aims to computationally investigate the crystallization induced by strain in polymer materials. Strain-induced crystallization is significant in various applications involving polymers. To effectively simulate this process computationally, the phantom model was employed to represent the polymer, and a specialized element formulation was developed using elastically inactive variables. These variables, which are undetermined through the phantom model's equations of motion, are interpreted as coordinate mappings for the material's configuration space. The material's crystalline content is calculated based on the kinetic version of the Erman-Viovy-Buehner model. A closed model for interchain stretching was also incorporated into the simulation. Simulation results show that the simulation accurately captures the material's response and successfully reproduces the characteristic stress oscillations observed in experimental data. Notably, localized regions of permanent crystalline content are found in highly coiled portions of the material's configuration space, which aligns with findings from previous simulation studies and experimental observations.

To analyze external magnetic field effects, we examined a nematic $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave superconductor with triplet Cooper pairs whose spins are aligned with the $z$ axis.
Our initial investigation of magnetic field effects along the $z$ axis revealed a Curie-law behavior, indicative of paramagnetism, with an effective magnetic moment that is significantly larger than a Bohr magneton by approximately two orders of magnitude.
When external magnetic fields were applied perpendicular to the $z$ axis, we found that the magnetic breakdown effect results in curvature in the Nernst coefficient and resistivity, while the paramagnetic behavior persists with the same Curie temperature regardless of the direction of the magnetic field.

A key advantage of Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) is its high resistance to fading in digital communication systems. To further improve this characteristic, we can utilize a differential CPM technique that compares a signal's symbol with a reference symbol. However, traditional methods to implement this technique face a limitation where the time required to detect a symbol equals the bit period, creating a performance lag. This paper presents a new approach to differential CPM detection that can increase this time requirement without affecting the detector's ability to distinguish signals, thus achieving enhanced delay capabilities. Furthermore, we develop a method to optimize this feature specifically. This new differential CPM detection technique can be effectively applied in delay-sensitive non-coherent DCPM communication systems.

A recent study proposed the idea that the quantum potential, initially introduced by David Bohm, can be equated to the compressibility of vacuum, providing support for the boSONization method employed to derive the cosmological constant. This study aims to give a more concrete and specific calculation of the quantum potential and compressibility of vacuum in the context of thermal systems with positive or negative temperatures.

Rule-based systems have regained popularity due to advancements in AI fields such as Explainable AI and Large Language Models. Constructing high-quality explanation rules requires comprehensive knowledge, and to facilitate this process, we need precise "then" statements and accurate situation descriptions that fully represent the problem at hand. To address these requirements, probabilistic models require training data reflecting real-world issue frequencies, and natural language models need datasets representative of actual problems to generalize effectively. In data science and NLP, a critical challenge is generating synthetic datasets with high fidelity to the underlying problems. Recent progress in creating knowledge graphs and rule-based systems has been hindered by using incomplete or inaccurate information, which limits the generalizability of models trained on such data. We propose ATOMIC, a 133,000-entry Atlas of Machine Common Knowledge comprising if-then statements and situation descriptions, and we investigate the limitations of generating synthetic datasets and the potential of graph-based knowledge in machine learning and natural language processing. Our study on reinforcement learning demonstrates that models trained on synthetic data struggle to apply their knowledge in new situations, whereas incorporating graph-based knowledge significantly enhances performance. Similarly, in NLP, replacing natural language explanations in ATOMIC with entity links limits the effectiveness of pre-trained models in applying their knowledge. These findings suggest that creating models capable of producing explanations that generalize effectively across a wide range of tasks is a crucial step towards achieving artificial intelligence.

As third-generation, near-term quantum computers start surpassing high-performance classical computers in specific tasks, the crucial challenge lies in utilizing them effectively. The development of efficient, practical quantum algorithms for financial applications is a key area of research in this context. This paper introduces NISQ-HHL, an innovative asset allocation framework that utilizes the quantum algorithm for resolving large-scale linear equations to achieve its objectives. We examine the original method's applicability to real-world, short-term quantum computers and refine it for this specific purpose. The NISQ-HHL approach leverages existing equity and bond assets as inputs, employing a heuristic transformation to linearize the tick data. To enhance practicality for short-term quantum devices, we also propose a refined, bond-based asset compared to the original method's theoretically unsuitable assets. Both the NISQ and NISQ-HHL algorithms are implemented on a short-term quantum computer, the QuEra Aquapod, in order to evaluate their performance in asset allocation. The results highlight suitable asset mixing strategies achievable through third-generation short-term quantum computers.

To improve low-resource languages with a high accent, developing accurate automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems is essential. To achieve this, an innovative, contact-tracing based, multi-modal ASR training method called BIdirectional Speech-Text FOCUS was used. This model incorporates two key components: a model that aligns audio and text models, and an attention mechanism that helps the model focus on critical parts of the input. Two types of loss functions were also tested to further refine the system's performance. Furthermore, research was conducted to examine the effect of delaying the model's model fusion model, which showed promising results. In experiments, the model outperformed baseline models significantly when working with models of differing sizes, showing improved results even when combined with larger models. These results indicate that the BIdirectional focus model can help create more accurate ASR systems for languages with limited data.

A sequence of uniform random parking functions with length n, as n increases, exhibits convergence in distribution to a specific limiting process that is uniquely determined. This limiting process is characterized by its finite-dimensional distributions and spatial properties, both of which are unique. Additionally, the empirical point process formed by the initial positions in these parking functions also converges to a unique limiting point process. We provide explicit descriptions for the limiting process and point process, and we establish the uniqueness for both. These findings extend previous findings that were only established for functions with specific properties, such as those being uniformly distributed.

The superconducting quantum interference effect holds immense potential for advancing quantum computing technology. To realize this, thin superconducting films must exhibit low disorder, thereby permitting precise control of Josephson tunneling through constrictions via electrostatic gating. Our study investigates the conductive properties of NbN nanowires with varying thicknesses in the context of the quantum phase-jump phenomenon and the Coulomb obstruction effect. Our findings reveal that a 2nm-thick NbN nanowire displays a distinct lack of coherence, whereas nanowires 3nm and 4nm thick exhibit well-defined quantum interference patterns. The energy gap measurements obtained from Little-Parks oscillations align with theoretical predictions, demonstrating the applicability of nanowire constrictions for implementing Josephson junctions in the context of quantum computing.

Predicting the movement of vehicles based on historical video footage is a crucial task for creating autonomous systems that can behave safely. To do this effectively, researchers focus on models capable of interpreting complex video sequences and predicting the future movements of vehicles within them. In order to tackle this challenge, we break down video sequences into a dual representation consisting of individual vehicle trajectories and inter-vehicle interactions, before testing a variety of frameworks that can process this data. As part of this investigation, we discover a novel, interaction-based attention mechanism suitable for vehicle forecasting, which can seamlessly integrate with widely used framework. When evaluated on the Berkeley Deep Drive dataset, our best performing approach successfully predicts the future movement of vehicles with high accuracy, outpreforming eleven comparable frameworks.

As we try to simulate biological enzymes and other complex molecules using quantum computers, it is essential to identify and account for various interorbital interactions that may influence our results. However, existing literature provides unclear guidance on the nature of these interactions, their characteristics, and their effects. This study aims to bridge the gap by examining interorbital interactions in detail, deriving theoretical expectations, and comparing them with quantum computer measurements. We specifically investigate bipartite graphs to demonstrate the Fock state symmetry and derive the universal interorbital relationship, then extend our findings to other graph structures. Our work paves the way for accurate bipartite graph simulations on bipartite lattices and other graph-based quantum simulations.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has -3 units of strangeness, was first theoretically predicted in 1963 but wasn't directly identified in any experiments until now.  
Discovering this particle would be a major milestone for QCD, as it would show that particles containing rare s-quarks can be made at collider machines like LHC.  
Recent studies of LHC data have mostly focused on particles with -2 units of strangeness, but the Ω-baryon, which has never been directly studied, needs to be confirmed as part of completing the task.  
The absence of Ω-baryon signals would narrow down the types of particles that can contain strange quarks and help limit theories beyond the Standard Model.  
This study encourages experimental collaborations to look for the Ω-baryon by analyzing LHC data, which would be a crucial step in fully understanding strange quark interactions.

Epidemics that spread through transportation networks in cities pose a significant challenge. These networks are intricate and ever-changing, making modeling and analysis difficult. A proposed framework called WellMix addresses these challenges by treating the bus system as a single, interconnected mixture model. This model incorporates three main components: streets, buses, and people, with models specifically tailored to each component's characteristics. By using a statistical approach, the framework can be easily updated as new data becomes available, providing reliable forecasts of the spread of infections on buses. These forecasts are evaluated and compared to other models, showing that WellMix offers valuable predictive capabilities. To further demonstrate the model's effectiveness, it is applied to forecast COVID-19 transmission on the Portland Transit Mall network. These results highlight the significance of the WellMix framework and provide a useful tool for public health officials and urban planners working with bus systems.

We investigated the spin-momentum current ratio efficiency in bismuth and cobalt multilayer films to better understand their potential in developing miniaturized spintronic devices. By adjusting the layer thickness, we discovered that precise control over the current ratio is feasible, with a minimum achieved at a total thickness of 4.5 nm. Analyzing the hysteresis loops and spin-orbit coupling-induced anomalous Hall effect revealed that spin-momentum currents can be enhanced through 20 equivalent periodic structures. Analyzing the spin-momentum currents revealed that boundary scattering plays a crucial role in determining the magnitude of the spin-orbit coupling in both in-plane and out-of-plane configurations, with an inverse relationship observed. By combining the two models, we were able to fit the experimental data and gain a deeper understanding of bismuth/cock multilayer behavior, which is essential for developing efficient magnetoelectronic applications.

This study presents exact solutions to the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in $N$ dimensions for a generalized Mie-type potential, denoted as $\frac{d_N V(r)}{d_N r} = \frac{a_N}{r^{1+\gamma}} + \frac{b_N}{r^\gamma} + c_N$, where $0 < \gamma \leq 1$, using the Jumarie fractional derivative method. By applying the fractional transformation, the problem was converted into an associated fractional differential equation, and a series of fractional semi-polynomial solutions were obtained through a fractional recurrence relation. Further analysis revealed a fractional recurrence relation for the normalization constants of the fractional wave functions. The analysis also establishes the fractional energy eigenvalues for the generalized Mie-type potential in $N$ dimensions.

We investigate the concept of neural network Lipschitz consistency, showing that it helps prevent overfitting and improves the reliability of models, particularly in scenarios where a model must make predictions beyond its trained data range. We demonstrate that enforcing a bound on the Lipschitz constant of a neural network can be viewed as an additional optimization constraint, and we develop a method to solve this problem using the inner-loop outer-loop (IOU) approach. To further simplify the calculations, we also introduce a neural tangent approximation that enables an efficient gradient-based solution to the IC constraint. Empirical results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in multiple areas, including preventing overfitting, detecting anomalies, and competing with top-performing consistency regularization techniques in vanilla vanilla adversarial training benchmarks. Our code is available online.

We investigate the Drell-Yan production of colorless bosons, like photons and Higgs bosons, through third-generation gauge vector leptoquark contributions at the LHC. Our study takes into account NLO QCD corrections using a comprehensive set of leptoquark+jet final states. Initially, we calculate the top-type leptoquark production cross sections for DY processes, then verify their robustness by comparing tree-level results with established lower bounds on exclusive processes. As anticipated, leptoquark effects on Drell-Yan photon production are minimal, with suppressed contributions of approximately 1% to 10% at various $\sqrt{s}$ values and kinematic conditions. In contrast, the bottom quark-initiated process dominates over the top leptoquark process for both photon processes. Simulations using PYTHIA 8 reveal that PVMLQ models can be constrained by experimental data on photon production accompanied by jets. Moreover, we find that PVMLQ models with very high mass thresholds could potentially explain the excess of high-$p_{T}$ di-photons unaccounted for by the SM.

In order to overcome excessive radiation exposure in PET imaging, this study introduces a novel, low-dose PET reconstruction method using a uncertainty-conscious, multivariate neural network. Unlike previous attempts using black-box neural networks, this study's approach is grounded in white-box statistical principles. We developed a start-point neural network that estimates variance for individual pixels and combines them to represent data spread, allowing the model to train on a small dataset while preventing overfitting. This study finds that the model's confidence levels differ between central and non-central data ranges, demonstrating its ability to adapt to data range changes in clinical trials. Furthermore, the model shows improved noise reduction, frame separation, and organ boundary definition compared to conventional methods, demonstrating its capacity to recognize and distinguish high-dose images from low-dose images and identify high-dose images with less accuracy. Additionally, the model's estimated data uncertainty aligns with actual pixel-wise residuals, demonstrating its statistical accuracy. Lastly, the model displays clinical translation potential with its clear, reliable uncertainty maps, demonstrating its ability to detect defective sensors and provide organ-level risk assessment in future studies.

Centralizing referents is a key aspect of how humans process language, according to Centering Theory. This approach suggests that the primary focus of a sentence is determined by the information that connects with the previous sentence. While this theory has been extensively used in computer-generated dialogue, recent research has examined its applicability to more complex forms of discourse, specifically in the context of neural coreference resolution. A new model was developed based on this research, integrating the concept of sentence centrality and a pre-trained neural network to identify connections between different expressions that refer to the same entity. This model, called CBT, achieved state-of-the-art results on two complex datasets, demonstrating the value of analyzing the primary status of expressions in resolving references.

The deployment of WiFi devices necessitates range assessment to determine effective coverage areas. Traditionally, this process involves range mapping by varying transmission power levels and measuring signal reception at various distances. However, this approach is time-consuming and intrusive. An alternative approach uses 3D packet distribution models to estimate range based on transmission distance. This paper aims to compare both approaches, the first involving direct measurement of range at different transmission power levels using a suitable protocol, and the second using packet distribution modeling, with results compared to existing literature.

The beam fragmentation instability significantly impedes high-current beam applications in energy recovery linacs. A new approach is presented that addresses its effects by optimizing the beam filling pattern within the structure. A detailed study on filling pattern optimization has been conducted using the PFIND beam fragmentation code, applied to a 500 keV to 1 MeV electron pre-collider application at an energy recovery linac. This analysis considers various beam filling patterns, including top-hat shapes with different widths and Gaussian patterns. It demonstrates that carefully selected top-hat patterns can enhance the beam current limit beyond what is possible with other patterns or without gaps, specifically in the context of an 115 keF0 photon gun and an ND endstation at an NEXUS endstation.

Our calculation determines the one-loop中点-emission vertex for two gluons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory within the fundamental representation of the gauge group. This is done using the $\mathcal{N}=4$ dual superamplitude's Witten amplitude representation. By applying the unitarity method, five-particle cuts of graviton-plus-gluon dual superamplitudes are calculated and then converted into an $\mathcal{N}=4$ amplitude with only a gap between the emitted gluons. To achieve this, an effective theory containing interactions between two gluons and two gravitons is constructed and then used to integrate the remaining $$\mathrm{PSU}(2|3)$$ supergroup degrees of freedom. Our calculation can also be verified by directly evaluating the maximally helicity violating (MHV)中点-emission vertex with the Lagrangian and applying the field-quantization method. Notably, our result is also proportional to the two-gluon seven-particle $$$\mathrm{NMHV}$$$$ dual superamplitude in the effective theory, but with a specific momentum configuration and with a particular color ordering of the emitted gluons that differs from the standard ordering by a phase factor. This relationship between the MHV and VMHV vertex is not an identity, but rather a specific proportionality under certain conditions.

This research examines the effects of surface friction on the behavior of molten polymer brushes with varying shapes, specifically linear and star-shaped configurations. By subjecting these configurations to high levels of friction, we observed that they undergo a transition from a melted state to a solid state, and undergo significant changes in surface structure and bulk properties. In particular, we discovered that linear configurations develop an "exclusion zone" at the foot of the configurations that increases in size as the shape becomes more elongated, and that these configurations also develop thick shells in close proximity to the surface and significantly altered properties in the region beyond the exclusion zone. We found that highly fragmented micelle structures within the thick shell contribute to increased surface density and that a feedback loop between surface density and monomer configurations beyond the exclusion zone that results in a significant increase in surface order and a substantial decrease in the size of the exclusion zone. As the configurations become more elongated, we observed that they develop a second, much thinner shell that is located beyond the first thick shell and that these configurations also undergo a notable decrease in the size of the exclusion zone and an increase in the thickness of the shell that is located beyond the first thick shell, and that this behavior is attributed to an interplay between shape-induced confinement effects and surface ordering. Overall, we found that surface friction has a profound effect on the behavior of molten polymer brushes and that their interactions can be used to significantly alter surface order and induce phase transitions in the bulk.

A subset of vertices in a graph G is considered resolvers when it helps to uniquely locate other vertices in the graph. The smallest size of such a subset is known as the metric dimension of G, which is denoted by $\beta(G)$. A scenario arises in which a specific method of identification is used for some of the graph's vertices, making them distinct from the rest, and the size of the locating subset needs to be minimized in this case, which is called the metric dimension with dominated target set. It was initially proposed by Acosta-Hernández et al. in 2019, and we will denote this variant as $\beta_T(G)$. In this study's objective, we confirm that the metric dimension is bounded by its shortened form, yet there is an exception to this rule, specifically for a type of graph called double star, which was also demonstrated in this study.

A new machine learning algorithm is introduced to process large astronomical datasets, specifically utilizing the Fermi-LAT all-sky map from 2008 to 2016. The model focuses on capturing time-varying patterns in astronomical images by training on simulation data and then applying it to actual observations. The assessment shows that the learned representation effectively differentiates between stable point clouds and objects exhibiting significant variability, outperforming other assessment methods. A key finding is the classification of TXS 2226066 as a highly fluctuating source, along with several other sources that have been identified and studied, including blazar, giant molecular clouds, and star-forming galaxies. The research highlights the suitability of machine learning models for analyzing dynamic astronomical phenomena using large datasets.

A serial dictatorship mechanism is considered equivalent to a class of time-based mechanisms, which allocate goods based on a specific ordering of agents, effectively mimicking a serial dictatorship for a subset of possible allocations. This paper introduces a mechanism that elicits agents' true preferences and achieves the same effect as a serial dictatorship mechanism, ensuring that lying goes unpunished and encouraging honesty among the participants. While this proposed mechanism is strategy-proof and efficient, it was not feasible to analyze its incentive compatibility.

We developed a streamlined approach to leverage the Pan-STARRS1 data catalog, streamining a 3.1 gigaparsec squared survey, to identify potential binary asteroids. Our method analyzes the time-varying positions of asteroids depicted in the five-color light curves recorded by Pan-STARRS1. This analysis focuses on anomalies in residual images after astrometric modeling, which can reveal signatures of binary systems. Applying our technique to 2700 minor planets with complete data, we found that 11 asteroids, listed as 2013 DM1, 2014 DE19, 2015 UU14, 2015 UU15, 2015 UU16, 2015 UU17, 2015 UU18, 2015 UU19, 2015 UU20, 2015 UU21, and 2015 UU22, exhibit behavior consistent with binary configurations. Notably, a closer examination of the anomalies present in the residual images of certain asteroids may provide valuable insights into their orbital dynamics and the physical characteristics of both primary and secondary components of the binary systems.

Large-scale data sets generated by online networks offer a rich source of variables for enhancing partial linear regression models. Researchers have explored the utilization of this information to identify significant confounding factors, develop novel instrumental variables, and refine covariance estimates in particular methodologies such as regression adjustment, Lasso, and instrumental variable analysis. This paper examines the theoretical validity of this framework, specifically in the context of network-based data, to establish a regression least squares estimator that converges at a $\sqrt{n}$ rate with consistency properties, and to develop an adjusted Lasso estimator with convergence rates surpassing traditional rates by one power of $\log(d_n)$ in both sparse and dense parameter spaces, and furthermore, in the latter space, it leverages this framework to create an instrumental variable estimator that achieves rates of convergence approaching the optimal bound.

Our research aims to enhance the user experience of text-based interactive narratives by instructing an AI to communicate and guide players in their virtual adventures. We specifically taught the AI Dungeon tool to engage players effectively and provide appropriate direction during a physical Dungeons & Dragons game with a human Dungeon Master and four D&D players. Our AI Dungeon Supervisor employs this unique capability of guiding the screen and navigating the keyboard to interact with the game. Communication skills were assessed through simulated D&D games, whereas our evaluation of the directing ability utilized think-aloud protocols. Our evaluation results indicate that our method of training the AI Dungeon Supervisor to communicate and provide direction is effective. Our findings are valuable for advancing the field of multi-agent learning in social contexts, particularly when it comes to communicating and directing screen-based users. We also discuss several practical applications of our results for further development of interactive narratives.

The intricate 3D structures of proteins are influenced by their primary amino acid sequences, a fundamental aspect of protein chemistry. While significant advancements have been made in unraveling the rules governing three-dimensional structures of regular molecules, the principles underlying the formation of complex, knotted structures remain poorly understood. Researchers believe that thermal fluctuations play a key role in the random coiling of proteins within confined spaces, a model that effectively explains the majority of proteins' structures. However, this model falls short in accounting for complex knots found in some proteins with regular structures. To bridge this gap, a study examined the configurations of an 8_18 knotted protein's random states, analyzing their topological properties by simplifying spatial complexities. The resulting topological models revealed regular patterns and symmetry, but also models that were entirely unknotted or features resembling local loops. These unusual configurations indicate specific random states as potential initial stages in forming the protein's final structure through controlled bending, a hypothesis further explored through analysis of another knotted protein and detailed molecular dynamics simulations.

We define symplectic mapping category groups for the blown-up tori in two dimensions, denoted as $\sigma(T^2_k)$. For the non-stable symplectic mapping categories of the blown-up tori, we define a specific notational representation, $\sigma(T^2_k)$, and demonstrate that this symbol, when colored red, exceeds the threshold of one. This mapping category symbol, in an orange hue, is also shown to be less than or equal to the binary logarithm of $k$ plus one. Additionally, we provide distinct examples of the symplectic mapping category, specifically showing that the blown-up torus with a single point, $\sigma(T^2_1)$, has a non-zero, but yet to be determined, specific value, and that the binary logarithm of $k$ plus one exceeds the lower bound of the symplectic mapping category for the blown-up torus with $2^n$ small symplectic curves.

A fundamental principle of quantum field theory is the irregular Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which asserts that the breaking of a continuous global symmetry always results in a specific, nontrivial vacuum current fluctuation associated with that symmetry. In quantum field science, these fluctuations are directly linked to the production of massless (or a very low mass) scalar particles that correspond to the breaking symmetry. In this report, we examine several well-known examples of both the regular and irregular types of Nambu-Goldstone phenomena across a wide range of theories, including Higgs-like models, non-Abelian gauge theories, and various nonrelativistic models. We particularly focus on a recently discovered non-irregular manifestation of the Nambu-Goldstone phenomenon in a nonrelativistic QED4 theory with a spontaneously broken scalar field, demonstrating that irregular jagged fluctuations exist even when the primary field is devoid of particles, and that this phenomenon is also present in the nonrelativistic QCD4 theory.

Modern language models excel at tasks requiring counterfactual reasoning, such as math and science, but they fall short with simple linguistic counterfactuals, like altering a sentence's meaning by replacing a phrase. This study investigates the origin of the models' ability to comprehend extensive language counterfactuals and develops a comprehensive framework called DISCO that explores the dimensions of subjectivity, propositional content, semantic relationship between original and alternative phrasings, and cognitive depth. By utilizing an arm's length substitution test and subject-specific prompt modifications, the researchers narrowed down the factors influencing the models' comprehension of linguistic counterfactuals to the phrasal relationship between the original and alternative statements, as well as the cognitive depth of the statement in question. Furthermore, they found that these models can even grasp subtle counterfactuals involving implicit information, as demonstrated by their performance on an implicit counterfactual dataset.

Epitaxial growth of a crystal can be divided into three categories: distant, dv, and pinhole, depending on how closely the lattices of the substrate and the film match. Combining different types of lattices in van der Waals substrates creates a range of ways that crystals can match their lattices. Graphene on an sapphire substrate has three ways to match its lattice due to its three-fold symmetry, creating three domains. We studied the equilibrium between these domains during the growth of a Heusler film and found that one domain creates distant epitaxy, while the other two create dv epitaxy. By adjusting the way the Heusler film starts to grow on each domain, we can control how dv and dv domains mix. This shows that van der Waals substrates can provide a wide range of ways to match lattices for growing high-quality 2D and thin films.

This code variant, known as $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear, was first introduced by K. R. Paramasamy and B. Parimala in 2017, extending our earlier introduction. These codes have an overall length represented by the sum $n+m$, a total rank denoted as $r$, and a minimum distance calculated using the GRS rank as $d=\max\{\frac{2r-n+m+2}2,\,r+\min\{n,m\}\}$. We've developed a decoding method for a specific configuration where $2r<n+m$, and also defined two essential properties for $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes: total rank and $\delta$-rank.

Supervising a model to distinguish between multiple possible outcomes based on the input and a single provided correct outcome is known as the partial label learning problem. Over time, this technique has gained popularity in various applications, including those where multiple outcomes are combined into one, such as text descriptions, images, or audio. Presently, we investigate partial label learning in the context of multiple outcomes, specifically exploring how models can be trained to properly handle situations where there are two possible outcomes combined into one. Using only this data, we compare the performance of various partial label learning techniques against baselines and find that the model's success heavily relies on its ability to learn from the individual outcomes. Furthermore, our analysis of the internal structure of a popular partial label learning model reveals insights into strategies for enhancing its performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating explanations can significantly improve the model's understanding of each outcome separately. However, this enhancement comes with the cost of requiring the provision of all possible outcomes.

Topological quantum field theories constitute an intriguing class of invariants that are computed via integrable models and knot theories, predominantly through number-theoretic and graph-theoretic methods. Recently, the concept of TQFT has been redefined using 2-functors from 2-nested complexes, encompassing a subset of naturally occurring data within the context of topological structures. Our investigation centers on a natural transformation between functors, identified as a module over a natural isomorphism, which we graphically represent using a specific diagram. This image of this module over a natural transformation, obtained through the integration process, yields the TQFT invariant in its simplest form. Through a step-by-step demonstration, we graphically derive the Pippard invariant of the Whitehead link as an application of this integral natural transformation, also known as a 2-categorical adjunction.

The origin of high-energy gamma-rays observed at the periphery of several nearby galaxies, such as the Milky Way and M31, remains a subject of speculation.  We propose that magnetic fields, generated during the periods that produce deep radio emissions, interact with intensely luminous accretion disks to explain these gamma-rays through synchrotron self-absorption and pair-production thresholds.  This explanation aligns with observed data and potentially accounts for the absence of 200 kevers absorption features.  As a result, we speculate that a variety of galaxies with deep radio emissions may have formed very high-energy components, potentially dark X-rays, associated with their ACCretion disks, captured by their magnetic fields.

The goal of this heart sound classification project is to classify healthy and abnormal sounds, which is crucial for early cardiovascular disease detection. To achieve this, 125 hours of heart sound recordings from five hospitals have been used, including those with recorded ambient noise. A comparison of different preprocessing techniques and machine learning models has been conducted to address the challenging semi-supervised and supervised classification problem. The research demonstrates that a simple approach, which involves extracting features and using a support vector machine, outperforms more complex deep learning models. The results obtained are particularly notable given the heterogeneous and partially missing nature of the dataset. The final model achieved high classification accuracy, reaching 92% F-score on training data and 85% F-score on test sets, which contain various heart conditions.

The rapid advancement of IoT technology has significantly transformed the field of healthcare, and the emergence of large-scale, wearable devices has given way to both convenience and data security challenges.  
To tackle these difficulties, wearable IoT healthcare systems require a breakthrough in PC-based diagnostics that possess three distinctive features: personalization, immediacy, and confidentiality.  
Federated learning holds the potential to provide a wearable IoT healthcare system with a shared, comprehensive, and secure diagnostic capability by enabling collaborative training across multiple learning devices without compromising data privacy.  
However, the existence of a vast knowledge gap between small, wearable devices and large-scale data sets, along with frequent knowledge transfer requirements between devices with different sizes, presents significant challenges for federated wearable IoT healthcare systems.  
To address these challenges, we introduce FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge structure for wearable wearable healthcare that capitalizes on the collaborative benefits of both federated learning and transfer learning.  
FedHealth demonstrates a wearable IoT healthcare system with a multi-layered structure for effective, external knowledge transfer, and through extensive simulations using real-world data, the effectiveness of FedHealth is validated in terms of its performance, efficiency, and security.

Recent years have seen a rise in the examination of portfolio characteristics that lead to better-than-average performance, with the aim of helping institutions design improved products and avoid unfair competition. However, a recent study by Brown, Ni, and Wang (2023) divides research into three main areas related to leading portfolios: by examining foreign options' impact on U.S. equity portfolios' highest returns, the tracking error minimization method for following asset classes with lower performance rankings, and the PRS selection criterion for following individual assets as benchmarks. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between tracking error and the squared multiple approach for creating portfolios that lead the market.

A challenge known as the "Now you see it, now you don't it" problem arises due to the
difficulty of managing computer software that is easily and frequently changing.
This problem is further compounded by the human element, as users often struggle
to effectively utilize powerful tools because of their inconsistent nature.
To mitigate the impact of these ever-shifting tools, computer programs have historically
been designed to interact with software in a more stable and user-friendly way,
by providing a consistent interface that remains largely unaltered, regardless of the
underlying tool's fluctuations.
Such interface wrappers have been extensively used in image processing and computer vision
for nearly four decades, with successful implementations including IDL's ImageToolkit,
GDPack for MATLAB, and the Interactive Data Language (IDL).
However, a notable absence is found in the realm of remote sensing,
where prominent packages like MATLAB and Python's GDA and AOSA for GIS are widely used,

Consider a variation of the optimal stopping problem where the agent suffers from a toggle effect and incurs additional, variable costs when changing decisions between stopping and continuing. The costs can change significantly, either abruptly or gradually, and must be taken into account from the second decision point onwards, which includes more intricate mathematical functions such as right-continuous or functions of bounded variation. By addressing this problem, we will be able to find optimal strategies to minimize total expected costs, the result of which can be represented in mathematical functions specific to this scenario, including variations of semimartingales and resolvents.

In order to address the muon g-2 anomaly, a new type of particle, a scalar leptoquark, is proposed, but to prevent unwanted interactions, another leptoquark of a different type must not be produced at high-energy colliders like the LHC. However, a careful analysis shows that even if there's an imbalance in the masses of these two leptoquarks, a minimal difference of 20 GeV allows for their pair-production to occur through the interaction of their momenta, leading to the discovery of this particle via its decay into two muons and a jet. The best fit for the data is found when the heavier leptoquark has a mass of 900 GeV and decays into the lighter one, which in turn decays into two muons and a jet.

We investigated the subthermal excitation of interstellar carbon monatomic lines within galaxies, emphasizing conditions where the energy required to emit these lines exceeds the ambient gas temperature. Although this requirement is typically met in the molecular gas reservoirs, we suggest that suggesting their presence as "forbidden" or "two-photon" transitions is misleading. These lines frequently arise from a subthermally excited state, and this overrepresentation of such terminology may be seen as deceptive. We contend that this subthermal excitation is highly relevant to understanding the energy transfer mechanisms within the cold phases of the interstellar medium and stress its importance. Furthermore, we highlight its potential utility, notably in imaging-based studies, where carbon monatomic lines could serve as effective tracers of low-temperature molecular gas, which is often missed by current surveys. This gas has been underrepresented in star formation analyses and may contribute to forming both low-mass and massive stars.

Researchers are using pulsar timing arrays to investigate the background gravitational waves produced by merging supermassive binary black holes. These arrays are sensitive to low-frequency gravitational waves, and a key challenge involves distinguishing between the stochastic background signals produced by these binaries. To address this challenge, we are set to generate catalogs of realistic, high-fidelity models of merging eccentric supermassive binaries. These models will be based on numerical relativity and include precise waveforms and efficiency energy outputs. Earlier models, which used effective potential techniques, produced lighter weight catalogs that are easier to manage. However, they are limited to binary systems with a mass ratio of less than 25 and have phase errors that exceed the tolerance of pulsar timing arrays near merger. In this study, we have used the Einstein@Home effective potential code to generate models with precise phase models for merging eccentric supermassive binaries for a specific eccentricity distribution. This model catalog is designed to be compatible with pulsar timing arrays and is publicly available for use. We also estimated the computational costs associated with generating and using this model catalog.

We establish a method to determine the speed at which particles move in an Asymmetric Simple Exclusive Random Walk on a one-dimensional lattice with a finite number of A_n root system symmetries. This technique enables us to either derive the velocity as a function of parameters for a specific walk corresponding to A_n, or to set bounds for walk variants where the number of particles is either unbounded or limited by the length of the line. This application yields new results in all three cases: an exact formula for the speed in A_n symmetric random walks with varying lengths, updated lower and upper bounds for A_n Potts model, and lower bounds for A_n random walks with a limited number of interactions.

Comprehensive epidemic modeling is now considered essential for managing outbreaks effectively. We examine key components integral to epidemic modeling, focusing on their use in modeling the current COVID-19 outbreak. We highlight critical elements such as model purpose, basic reproduction number, R0, contact tracing, quarantine protocols, non-pharmaceutical interventions, NPIs, and superspreading events. We also examine how various models have been used to analyze the COVID-19 outbreak and discuss both their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, we explore emerging topics in epidemic modeling, including the integration of spatial dynamics, behavioral changes, host immunity, and co-occurring infections. We believe these complex subjects require continued research to fully understand and address the risks posed by infectious disease outbreaks.

Recently, new techniques for creating molecules from spinor atoms have been developed, despite relatively small theoretical predictions. Through extensive three-body recombination experiments conducted with Na atoms, our research explores both the molecules formed and the underlying factors affecting them. Our post-processing method, utilizing recombination rates measured at various temperatures, enables precise recovery of final particle populations, allowing for in-depth analysis of molecules formed. It was discovered that most of the molecules are produced in highly excited states close to their dissociation threshold, rather than in the lowest energy state. Furthermore, our study found evidence of a specific three-body collision process, resulting in a single molecule and two excited atoms. This collision process, which can match or surpass the well-known two-body loss process in magnitude, produces molecules with significant kinetic energy and atoms that contribute to unaccounted wall losses, manifesting as temperature-independent wall losses above approximately μK temperatures. These molecules and atoms are primarily generated through a two-body process induced by an external magnetic field, as indicated by our analysis of loss rates in relation to magnetic field variations. Ultimately, our research provides an exhaustive characterization of three-body recombination, offering valuable insights for the development of molecules from ultracold atomic gases via two-body loss-induced wall collisions.

Bipartite graphs are commonly used to depict information about things, like social networks and organizational structures. However, manipulating the hierarchy and information within these representations can be cumbersome and inefficient. A new method is presented that leverages a unique DNA data encoding and error correction scheme, specifically a (3, 8, 3)-erasure correcting HDI tree-assisted DAG (3, 8, 3) code, to write and retrieve both the information and the DAG's hierarchical structure directly from storage. Research conducted on both simulated and real hardware shows that this method is feasible and efficient, with the capacity to correct up to three data node insertion/deletion errors and three edge disruption errors, ensuring high reliability in retrieving the desired information. The results also highlight the practicality of using DNA data structures that can be manipulated in a hierarchical and informational sense.

PREDICE, or the Predictive Computational Intelligence Engine, is a novel framework that integrates four key components: a neural operator to learn the governing physics of a system, another neural operator to project solutions onto an extended functional space, an ensemble of solutions to ensure accuracy, and boundary conditions applied to a single, continuous domain. This framework can be trained to accurately model a wide range of fluid dynamics problems, and we specifically demonstrate its efficacy in modeling the shallow water equations. The efficacy of PREDICE is shown through several benchmarks, including dam break, river flow, and river-lake interactions, and it achieves remarkable speed improvements of up to four orders of magnitude compared to traditional numerical methods.

Neural networks excel in various tasks but struggle with generalization under new conditions. Our causal framework outlines three major ways to train neural networks: empirical, structural, and extrinsic learning. We examine how data can be structured, the connections and conflicts between these methods, and their practical applications. This approach classifies typical neural learning techniques like EPITECH and STRETCH, and suggests promising directions for research. We validate our causes framework by exploring six causal variables present in six widely used neural learning algorithms. As an example, we build and compare neutral networks using learning methods that reflect their underlying causal structures. This research direction is promising, yet challenging, so we call for projects that develop, test, and integrate these methods.

This note explores a concept called the b-principle, which is discussed in the context of complex geometry. We reference additional research that supports or challenges the b-principle, particularly research by Banakara, Clift, and Das who proved it in a specific case, and research by Tan who found it doesn't hold in a more general scenario.

Understanding how fluids interact with deformable biological tissues is crucial for comprehending various physiological and pathological conditions, including issues with the heart's heart. Successfully simulating these phenomena on a computer requires complex mathematical models that are solved using numerical methods on multiple overlapping grids of different sizes. However, efficiently solving the resulting equations is hindered by the poor scalability of traditional numerical techniques specifically for the solid mechanics component of this model. We've developed a new set of multilevel solvers to overcome these limitations by adapting existing geometric tools to a specific type of commonly used model for heart mechanics (the active stress model). Our approach is examined through various tests on realistically shaped grids representing the ventricle of the heart, comparing our results with existing multilevel solvers and demonstrating improved performance and scalability for standard physiological simulations.

This research investigates the correlation between the growth of mean squared displacement and time in flow through porous media with randomly distributed permeability. We identify three distinct diffusion regimes - subnormal, normal, and supernormal - and focus on the spread of leading-edge particles exhibiting power law behavior. The research finds that the exponents for these power law regimes offer more reliable indicators of randomness than the overall diffusion types. Furthermore, it demonstrates that when the distribution of local Péclet numbers is symmetric, the exponents for the subnormal and supernormal regimes are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, providing five reliable rules that link these indices to the randomness of the permeability distribution's tails.

A key step in developing a model for a waveguide-resonator system's optical behavior involves obtaining analytical expressions for the modes of both the resonator and waveguide, as well as their nonlinear interaction term, which arises due to the Kerr effect. While this can be achieved through various methods, our approach offers the most straightforward and general way to do so by leveraging Maxwell's equations in their integral form. This method bypasses the need to make assumptions about the variation of the electric field, allows for an arbitrary distribution of dielectric constants, and thus enables precise expression of both linear and nonlinear interaction terms in terms of mode coefficients with no unknown proportionality constants. Our model validates previous findings and extends beyond them, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the optical properties of these systems.

DL technologies, particularly reinforcement learning (RL), have been widely applied in various fields, including finance, healthcare, and manufacturing. While RL models show promise, their reliability remains in question due to the lack of rigorous performance testing. Although benchmarking has been established for supervised learning, RL evaluation remains fragmented. To bridge this gap, we present RLDB, a specialized reinforcement learning database that replicates RL evaluation practices across industries. Although named initially as L2Explorer to reflect its purpose of exploring the "second layer" of applications behind the "second hand' of time, we encourage the name RLDB for its broader relevance. Key features of the L2Explorer include over 40 classic and cutting-edge RL algorithms, a diverse array of stationary and non-stationary environments, a modular plugin system, and a user-friendly interface. As an open-source framework, the L2Explorer encourages the research and development of RL reliability through rigorous testing.

For highly resilient and efficient software frameworks, the use of surveillance and exploration techniques has been strongly advocated, which were initially proposed by Heiss et al in 2022. Their method, known as Peeking, is designed to facilitate such practices in declarative processes by combining the powers of stream operators. However, this text-based approach limits the applicability of the technique in various practical scenarios. The goal of our project, Kiosk, is to make the declarative approach more user-friendly and accessible by integrating the Peeking method. To achieve this, we've added a cutting-edge interface that enables the creation of interactive dashboards and the incorporation of unobserved data through the 'peeking' method. To support these features, Kiosk relies on the integration of the Process Mining Package and R's native graphics capabilities. The proposed method's effectiveness will be further demonstrated through a detailed examination of its application to real-world datasets, including the generation of illustrative dashboards, the discovery of concealed patterns, and the utilization of supplementary data sources.

Consider a subset of the positive real numbers, denoted as $s$, and another subset of the product of these numbers, denoted as $K_s(\mathbb{R}^n)$. These subsets are defined based on their resistance to deformation under certain conditions. We are now extending the definition of this subset by incorporating a new type of number, denoted as a finite or infinite power of an infinitesimally small positive number $s$. This extension results in a corresponding set of numbers, denoted as $\Theta$, which includes the original set of numbers $\{1\}$, the positive real numbers $\mathbb{R}_+$, and additional sets based on powers of $s$. For each of these sets, we define their respective subsets of the product of non-negative real numbers, denoted as $K_\sigma(\mathbb{R}_+^n)$. We then prove that these subsets are algebraically expressible and provide algorithms to do so. This has the beneficial effect of allowing for an exact representation of their boundaries using algebraic methods. These compactifications of the space of parameters have the potential to be utilized in the study of families of polynomial and trigonometric equations, as well as in the analysis of certain types of dynamical systems.

Extended simulations with BBN+ (build bulges from binaries and stars physics) applied to galaxies up to $10^{10} \ \mathrm{L}_{\sun}$ explore the connection between galaxies and supermassive black holes, and the role of star-forming binaries in creating massive black holes and star-forming bulges. A sample of 424 simulated galaxies is examined to determine if a relationship exists between the total black hole mass and star formation in galaxies, and if star-forming binaries contribute to quenching star formation in galaxies with high mass. A weak correlation is found between the total black hole mass and log of specific star formation rate, but no strong connection is evident on individual massive galaxies with active star formation ($\mathrm{SFR} \times \mathrm{t}_{\sun} > 0.7$). However, a strong negative correlation is discovered when focusing solely on the bulge black hole mass and specific star formation rate in these massive galaxies, indicating that a significant portion of the total black hole mass can quench star formation in massive galaxies. Furthermore, the study indicates that star-forming binaries can give rise to massive black hole binaries that activate jets and gamma-ray bursts, expelling gas and inhibiting further star formation in these galaxies. A potential observational test of this theory is examining the presence of gamma-ray bursts or active galactic nuclei in star-forming bulges of massive galaxies with ongoing star formation.

For ease of use, consumers frequently rely on multilingual reviews to form opinions about products and services.
To make informed decisions, it is crucial to accurately determine the sentiment expressed in reviews from languages other than their own.
This study introduces a novel task, cross-lingual sentiment evaluation, which involves determining the emotional intensity behind statements whose underlying language is unknown, by utilizing training data with emotional intensity labels for that specific language.
By using this approach, we demonstrate that utilizing labeled emotion intensity data enhances performance in the subsequent assessment phase, on statements from the same languages.
Furthermore, by comparing our results with those of baseline models, we found that even minimal amounts of emotion intensity data can positively impact performance in determining emotional intensity of statements from the same languages.
While the primary goal of this study is to analyze the challenges of determining emotional intensity in statements from the same languages, our findings also have implications for more traditional multilingual sentiment analysis models.

Studies indicate that Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can effectively classify COVID-19 cases, often indistinguishable from healthy individuals or those with pneumonia. However, it remains unclear whether CNNs can also distinguish between patients with COVID-19 who require ICU support and those who they do not. This study aims to explore this knowledge gap.

The concept of a simplicial bundle was first introduced by Whitehead in 1948 and later re-introduced by W. Massey in 1961. Over the course of two sections, this article aims to compare and contrast the definitions of a simplicial bundle provided by these two authors. Along the way, we introduce the definition of a change of simplicial decomposition and establish the fact that a simplicial bundle can be characterized in terms of a local triviality condition that mirrors the local properties of a simplicial complex. Additionally, we prove that a global simplicial structure can be achieved through a specific type of pullback.

This paper delves into the challenge of visual association detection (VAD), paying particular attention to the problematic issue of false positives caused by the co-occurrence of unrelated objects within images. We propose a new, challenging dataset called Visual Association Chunks (VAC), comprising 15,000 images that mask the associations between the involved objects to a degree where unrelated (FP) and related (LR) status are evident even to human observers. In contrast, FP samples prove exceedingly difficult for standard visual association models to distinguish from LR samples, leading us to develop a novel baseline approach that explicitly leverages both parts of the VAC dataset. Building upon this baseline, we explore various techniques drawn from the realms of contrastive learning and data augmentation to further enhance VAD models. It is worth noting that our findings offer valuable insights and a practical reference for researchers aiming to address the frequent but underutilized issue of EPs in computer vision tasks. We have made the VAC dataset publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhixuanzhang/VAC.

Cosmological models suggest that massive galaxies experienced significant bursts of star formation and black hole growth during a specific period, which occurred between the ages of 2 and 4 billion years. During this time, these black holes were thought to have been fed by massive inflows of gas, while at the same period, many massive galaxies also experienced a merging of smaller galaxies that had formed early on. In an effort to understand how events like black hole activity and the merging of galaxies contributed to these intense bursts, researchers carried out sophisticated simulations of a galaxy group known as SDSSJ1039+1700. During a specific 200 million years period within this galaxy group, a burst of black hole activity and an increase in the amount of early-type galaxies were observed, which coincided with one of the galaxies experiencing a merger that led to an increase in its total mass and a shift towards older stellar populations. Furthermore, this merged galaxy contributed a substantial amount of gas that fueled a period of intense star formation and the creation of a massive elliptical galaxy at the center of the galaxy group.

On November 7, 2004, seven space-based neutron monitors recorded the lowest threshold events ever classified as G1 solar ground level events. This unusual occurrence took place in the direction of a massive solar flare, rated X2.0. A thorough examination of the observed neutron events was carried out by analyzing their energy spectra and timing patterns. Notably, a significant discrepancy between the space-based and ground-based recording systems' timing patterns was discovered, which could be attributed to the movement of the solar event towards the Earth's direction. Furthermore, the energy spectra recorded showed a unexpected lack of high-energy particles, a pattern that was replicated across multiple recording sites but was also seen in other extensive solar particle events of similar magnitude. This replicated pattern could not be linked to the main massive solar flare, leading to the hypothesis that it was caused by a minor, narrow-angle particle beam that originated from a small solar compact filament.

A growing number of exoplanets with tidally locked status indicate signs of angular angular momentum being transferred in unexpected ways. This phenomenon is particularly evident in SPBoCom planets, which show a high level of thermal emission on their night sides. In a new study, we examine 17 hot Saturns and Jupiter class planets undergoing hot spot phase curves, extracting valuable information on albedo patterns and emissivity from phase curve analysis. We find that the maximum intensity of emitted light is not always aligned with the hottest point on the planet, which is a hallmark of spatial variations in emissivity. Additionally, we observe discrepancies in minimum values of albedo and emissivity across different wavelength ranges, which is a sign of complex absorption patterns. These complex spatial variations in emitted light imply that a significant amount of angular momentum is being transferred, which is a key indicator of atmospheric dynamics. In an effort to explain the observed behavior, we employed a sophisticated 3D radiative hydrodynamic model, which reveals that the magnitude of angular momentum being transferred is consistent with the extreme temperature differences experienced by giant gas planets near their orbits. Uniquely, the model also shows that complex absorbing patterns cannot be explained by common compounds such as water vapor, carbon monoxide, methane, or ammonia, which is a call to identify new molecules that may thrive in the atmospheres of giant gas planets.

The rapid proliferation of social media and online news platforms has given rise to a booming industry of counterfeit news, which poses a significant threat to public safety and welfare. Due to the vast amount of information available, manually verifying news authenticity is an impractical task, necessitating the development of a scalable automated solution for emergent counterfeit news detection. However, existing methods fall short as they rely on limited identification information about content creators, which restricts their effectiveness in capturing the full scope of risk associated with newly appearing sources. In this paper, we investigate a more challenging scenario where the source information about content creators is limited, and we develop a novel solution called Meta NCP that leverages our network-based risk assessment framework to detect counterfeit news in emergent sources. Through extensive experiments on a large-scale dataset, we show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches and manully crafted baselines, providing a robust and adaptable solution for emergent counterfeit news detection.

This research project examines how solutions to a recurrent transport equation change under different initial conditions, particularly when these conditions don't adhere to a specific symmetry. We show that under certain conditions, the functions describing this equation's outcomes are discontinuous in a way that isn't smooth, even when the parameters being varied are continuous. These findings hold true under quite general conditions and can be applied to understand the behavior of a model known as the Lorentz gas with a specific type of recurring behavior. In this model, we found that the relationship between the time it takes for a particle to return to its original state and the size of that particle is discontinuous in size, and this lack of smoothness is essential to understanding what happens when the size of the particle increases beyond a certain point and it no longer returns to its original state in a continuous manner, and this understanding is relevant to another model with a similar structure.

This study proposes novel multi-phase coding sequences for improved radar performance, drawing on Golay complementary design principles. Initial findings present four-phase designs, including both orthogonal and non-orthogonal variants, based on diagonal matrices with distinct phase angles. Sixteen optimal three-phase designs are discovered, all sharing the same cliquet level, and classified into two distinct categories: a main cluster of designs related through unitary transformations and a secondary group with completely different structures. Finally, an extensive design with one hundred and four three-phase subsets is identified, all nested within a larger two-phase structure, and offered for enhanced radar application performance.

Silicon situated in its pure state exhibits four two-fold coupled valleys in the conduction band with varying effective masses and orientations. When silicon is constricted, these valleys begin to decouple and their interaction can lead to localized states with distinct energy levels and increased effective masses along specific crystallographic axes. This property makes decoupled silicon highly suitable for enhancing transport characteristics in field-effect transistors and facilitates the development of functional devices incorporating decoupled silicon through techniques like silicon nanowire inversion, nanomembranes, and nanowires. In this research, scientists probed valley interaction in an isolated silicon nanomembrane and discovered localized states with modified effective masses and anisotropic behavior along different nanomembrane axes. They also demonstrated controlled manipulation of two types of quantum particles - electrons and nuclear spins - by utilizing external electric and magnetic fields, including the transfer of spin information to electrons via controlled application of voltage. The findings highlight the potential of decoupled silicon nanomembranes for creating robust and scalable quantum devices.

Simple, sparsifying graph representations are fundamental to many complex systems, including our own brains. Though research has explored representation learning and architecture discovery in a separate areas of focus, this work addresses both areas simultaneously. Our approach uses a novel graph neural network that learns representations and an adjacency function to construct a initial graph, which is then refined through an external optimizer to maximize task performance. We evaluate this end-to-end method on two distinct problems: a benchmark synthetic scenario and a complex, real-world mooring system with unknown dynamics, achieving superior results in comparison to a tree-based network in both instances.

Generating realistic brain lesions on healthy images is a crucial step in creating realistic training data for medical image analysis tasks that require inputting damaged images.  Previous studies that used real brain images with lesions as training data could be scaled up with the help of algorithms that generated synthetic lesions.  However, often these generated lesions looked unnatural and distorted the underlying healthy images in unrealistic ways.  Our proposed model focuses on creating synthetic lesions that preserve the images' underlying content while being diverse and randomly generated.  We found that when we 1) restricted our generation process to the most prominent frequency components of the input images and 2) incorporated a generation sequence into our framework, the resulting images with synthetic lesions were highly indistinguishable from real images with lesions, as demonstrated by both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.  Our model was also able to generate diverse synthetic lesions in the same image at multiple different locations, sizes, and shapes, and was able to replicate the statistical distribution of lesions found in a publicly available dataset.  Our research can significantly aid the development of a diverse set of brain images with lesions for training purposes, and has a wider applicability to other diagnostic images.

A significant update to the GP-2 PostProcessor compiler was made by Richard V. Snellings in 2004, which considerably expanded its initial capacity. The revised version of the compiler is now able to handle option flags, automatic parameter setting, and comment inclusion. The compiler is written in Fortran 90 and is specifically tailored to work with Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X systems. GP-2 is also distributed alongside GWO, a program used for generating random walker trajectories. The compiler's functionality is demonstrated through the simulation of random walker trajectories as an example.

External resources such as knowledge graphs, K-cores, and pre-annotated attributes significantly facilitate machine translation, information extraction, and other NLP tasks by reducing the need for training data. Recently, attention-based models have been able to effectively identify important parts from unstructured text, leading to the development of separate systems for various types of attribute extraction - name-level, phrase-level, and statement-level. However, in our work, we propose a novel network structure that unifies this variety by UNITE, which employs simple dual networks trained to recognize importance through contrastive learning, achieving remarkable results on multiple benchmarks and outperforming previous models across different evaluation metrics.
