Not recently, a variety of studies on deep learning have been highly successful in image classification tasks, yet there is still a lack of availability for trained models that can accurately detect malignant skin lesions. Malignant skin lesions, medically referred to as melanoma, are the most deadly form of skin cancer and if left untreated with early diagnosis and treatment, melanoma has the highest cure rate among all types of cancer affecting the skin. The research team's proposed model combines a deep learning architecture known as Residual Convolutional Neural Network (ResCNN) with an anomaly detection technique called One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM) to accurately classify skin images and identify melanoma. In the training process, normal samples are excluded from the dataset, and the model is trained solely on atypical images. A critical component of this study is a new, large-scale dataset consisting of 109,698 images across five categories of skin cancer, labeled according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 classification system. When evaluated on this comprehensive dataset, the proposed model outperformed existing methods in classifying melanoma with the following performance metrics: sensitivity of 0.99, precision of 0.99, and F1 score of 0.99.

A horizontally placed, rapidly spinning Hele-Shaw cell containing a viscous fluid and a non-wetting air bubble above it fosters strong Rayleigh-Taylor and Coriolis forces. This setup is used to simulate flexible finger patterns that emerge during fluid dynamics. Experimental data supports this claim.

This study estimates the amounts of several molecules, specifically cyclopentadiene (C5H5), ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH), and cyclopropenyl acetylene (C3H2CCH), in the TMC-1 cloud using radiative transfer modeling. A notable discovery is that two distinct forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, cis-ethynyl cyclopentadiene and trans-ethynyl cyclopentadiene, coexist and are present in roughly equal amounts with a combined abundance that is about 10 times greater than that of cyclopropenyl acetylene. Furthermore, there is a higher abundance of unsaturated bonds in these molecules compared to other isomers like cyclopropenyl acetylene. These estimates indicate that a significant portion of hydrogen atoms in aromatic and unsaturated bonds are found within hydrocarbon cycles. Additionally, a method for calculating the equilibrium constants of a chemical reaction is proposed, which can be used to determine the ratio of the two ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers and is found to be close to 1 based on modeling of TMC-1.

Neural machine translation models have gained significant advancements due to the look-ahead information they can access during the generation process. However, such techniques are difficult to transfer to models for creation tasks like generation, due to the lack of parallel data required for their training. In order in order to make progress on difficult generation tasks that involve a vocabulary mismatch, we investigate the potential of using look-ahead information from VLM models. Our proposed method, named "Focus on predicted word candidates in the future" (FAF), employs the predicted vocabulary from an auxiliary model to prioritize word attention in its generation. FAF achieves notable improvements over baseline models that use the same amount of data, resulting in a 5 to 10 percent increase in METEOR scores when evaluated on five under-explored language pairs. Furthermore, it demonstrates improved efficiency by reducing model parameters and preprocessing time, as well as enhancing speed during the generation phase. Additionally, the proposed method is capable of generating high-quality translations when given access to predicted vocabulary from state-of-the-art post-editing models, resulting in a 20 to 30 percent decrease in post-editing time required.

The framework concept for computer systems was first introduced by Davis and I in 2010, providing a novel perspective on designing and building highly parallel systems. This approach emphasizes designing abstract interfaces that are technology-neutral, thus making frameworks adaptable to various underlying technologies. Although the framework concept is a theoretical construct, a similar construct called the Grid Software Framework (GSF) was developed by the Berkeley Grid Computing Group in the late 1990s. We present a post-mortem analysis of GSF's architecture and underlying philosophy, which we argue was primarily a cluster computing framework. This presentation of GSF through the lens of our framework concept offers readers a distinct perspective compared to existing presentations. Additionally, our interactive version of GSF, available at https://github.com/daviddoescode/grid, presents a working model of the architecture.

A new 'combined' dark sector model is proposed with three distinct and non-interacting components: dark energy that dissipates energy, dark energy without dissipation, and dark matter. This model is assessed using observational data, including Hubble parameter data from various radius of curvature measurements, low-redshift data, Cosmic Microwave Background data, and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect data. Parameter estimation is performed using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MPC) methods, and the equation of state evolution is analyzed. The model's equation of state evolves from matter-like behavior in the early universe to a liquid state in a transitional phase, and finally to a gaseous state in the late universe. Comparisons are also made with other dark sector models.

Our research investigates the effective field theory of neutrinos and scalar dark energy, searching for beyond-Standard-Model contributions to the decay of $J/\psi$ into photons and invisible particles. In the neutrino sector, we calculate a one-loop correction to this decay process, finding that the resulting contribution is too small to be significant given current experimental constraints. In the scalar dark energy section, we consider tree-level contributions to the same decay, discovering that they are suppressed and too minuscule to be meaningful. Both forms of physics produce neutrino contributions that are heavily limited, with cross-section values well below their bound set by the decay width of $J/\psi$.

Dimensional analysis has long been a valuable tool for developing mathematical models that accurately reflect the physical world's inherent relationships between variables and dimensions. A novel approach combines machine learning, specifically support vector regression, with traditional dimensional analysis to create a more robust modeling technique. This integration enables the development of accurate mathematical models, even when working with complex, continuously varying data sets that include both single-variable and multi-variable components representing curves, surfaces, and other geometric shapes. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of our novel approach, focusing on challenging high-dimensional data sets, and presents engaging case studies across a range of applications, including biological, mechanical, and geophysical functional datasets.

The concept of a random walk with persistent behavior is well-established in the context of multidimensional spatial diffusion and also applies to the duration a particle spends at a specific location in one-dimensional random walks. This paper investigates various random walk models to identify those that exhibit persistent properties, defined as the prolonged duration a particle spends at a particular site in one-dimensional space. A simple persistent random walk with biased turns demonstrates persistent duration, characterized by a probability distribution that decays at a power law rate. Conversely, both the persistent symmetric simple random walk and the local duration of the fractional Brownian motion-driven random walk do not show persistent duration for any parameter values. This study provides comparative analyses of these models' statistics and theoretical foundations.

The helicon plasma source is highly effective for producing high-density plasmas, making it well-suited for simulating various types of plasma thruster experiments. The IShTAR facility will be able to simulate Hall thruster discharges with the helicon source to simulate a wide range of thruster powers up to 20 kW. A mathematical analysis of the helicon plasma source was carried out in the IShTAR device to a determine its power capacity. The analysis showed that the power threshold occurs at the balance between helicon plasma mode and low frequency sheath mode, the power beyond this threshold is linearly proportional to the 1.15 exponent of the magnet field strength. The next step is to measure the plasma characteristics with the helicon source to compare with the theoretical analysis.

The microscopic examination of biological tissue images is a key method for diagnosing diseases, yet it relies on skilled pathologists who manually examine cellular components, including the nuclei of cells.  The scarcity of experienced professionals and the high cost of their services have spurred interest in developing a reliable, nucleus-detection system using image processing technology.  Nucleus detection is particularly difficult due to the similar appearance of nuclei and surrounding tissue, as well as the wide diversity in their size, shape, and color. To address these challenges, we have created a novel nucleus detection system that combines deep convolutional networks to automate the annotation process and thoroughly identifies nuclei in biological tissue images. Our system, which we call W-Net, employs a two-stage process: the first stage divides images into nuclei, background, and ambiguous areas, while the second stage classifies each pixel into nuclei or background with the assistance of training data annotated by both experts and the output of the initial stage. Our approach, which can be efficiently fine-tuned to meet different processing requirements, has been tested on three publicly available datasets and demonstrates superior performance compared to other leading methods.

We establish the local converse theorem for all irreducible components of the Bessel and Fourier coefficients for all odd special orthogonal and symplectic symplectic groups of type OSp(2n+1,F).

For a field F with a characteristic not equal to two, where it lacks certain traits, we define the maximal extent of the relevant groups as 2*(min(n_O, n_Sp)). When the product of the lengths of two sets of distinct integers and their corresponding minimal products exceed this extent, the two sets and their products are unique.

This uniqueness property holds for all collections of integers that define the modularites of certain Bessel and Fourier coefficients of all unitary representations of these groups that are relatively compact.

Our result builds on prior work by Jiang and Soudry as well as Lin, Ma, and Nan.

Our research also holds relevance for distinguishing between different modular representations of these groups that are relatively compact.

Additionally, we prove that the certain Bessel and Fourier coefficients are not empty for all OSp(2n+1,F).

This result is important for applying the OSp(2n+1,F) rainbows as well as the distinguishing principle to these groups in the setting where the characteristic is not two.

Deep learning techniques, particularly graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), have gained prominence due to their remarkable performance. However, the underlying principles of GCNNs remain enigmatic, particularly the role of the K-harmonics filtering component. In this work, we investigate the essential functionality of GCNNs and provide a more basic interpretation of the model. Our research reveals that the non-linear activation function in GCNNs serves a critical purpose in facilitating the learning of feature transformations. Additionally, we found a direct correlation between K-harmonics filtering and matched filtering methods on graph Laplacian eigenfunctions, which act as efficient filters on graphs. To support our theoretical findings, we conducted experiments that demonstrate the GCNN model's superior performance compared to a linear GCNN variant.

By applying a saddle-point approximation to a large N expansion, we examine the classical field theory that emerges from a topological complex scalar field with a spin-like chemical potential, defined on anti-de Sitter space with a linearly growing gravitational metric. Through the imposition of boundary conditions and the integration of degrees of freedom at the edge of the system, we edge-mode gauge/gravity duality reveals a two-dimensional Einstein-Cartan theory with a positive sign for the cosmological constant. Solving the bulk topological complex scalar field with spinning black hole and soliton vacuums as starting points, we find that in both cases the edge degree of freedom becomes nontrivial. Notably, solitons correspond to the critical point of the black holes, marking the phase transition boundary. A phase transition between hairy black holes and solitons occurs as the spinning black hole's phase space is divided into these two states by this transition point, akin to liquid and gas phases in thermodynamics. However, no edge degree of freedom is produced when the spinning black hole reaches an infinite radius, signaling a phase transition and generating a new vacuum state known as solitons that divides the entire set of possible boundary conditions into two parts with opposite topological properties.

Cross-scale elastography imaging is a key method for assessing an individual's muscle and tissue properties. However, its precision relies heavily on accurate estimation of the displacement field, which can be challenging to achieve due to the influence of shear waves and bulk sound waves that cause distortions in the measured data. In order to improve the accuracy of these elastography images, it is essential to improve the estimation of axial and lateral sound wave measurements. Focusing on the often overlooked lateral dimension, this study investigates two synthetic aperture reconstruction algorithms, including a newly developed one called virtual origin synthetic aperture. When applied to both simulated and experimental data, this new algorithm outperformed the other one in terms of computing efficiency. Furthermore, it was found that using a side lobe filtering method in combination with this VOSA algorithm yielded the most accurate results.

The concept of Rational Action Models has been introduced, building upon the analysis of rational behavior in current AI presentations. We propose an alternative to current method demonstrations in presentations, called Rational Pseudocode, which focuses on explaining the underlying logic behind an algorithm rather than its execution. The framework consists of four key components: acknowledging human limitations, creating simplified analogies, discarding unnecessary details, and presenting step-by-step procedures. This approach is illustrated using examples such as the PageRank presentation and the MoE demo. Additionally, we discussed the benefits of this method and provided suggestions for further research. We believe this presentation will be most impactful for a target audience comprising present-day AI professionals.

The efficacy of unsupervised learning methods heavily relies on the accuracy of models they produce, which, in the case of a growing amount of input information, is often compromised by excessively complex models. Such overfitting issues are addressed by versatile algorithms that prioritize simplicity, yet currently lack the ability to adapt to changing information dimensions, a limitation this research aims to overcome. This work introduces two novel dynamic groupings methods, the Simple Dynamic Relevance Tree and the Multi-classify Simple Dynamic Relevance Tree, that facilitate an optimal scale of information segmentation by automatically adjusting partitions and facilitating multi-classification, resulting in recommendations that are nearly as effective as the most complex possible models while maintaining a high level of simplicity. Statistical analysis and information optimization principles are used to validate the reliability of these methods, which are demonstrated through various real-world applications including web page recommendations, web image searches, and mobile app recommendations.

A new approach to analyzing deterministic and stochastic pursuit-decision games is presented, which involves hierarchical breakdowns of these games based on the strategies used by players. The paper demonstrates that under certain strategy types, significant subdivisions can be found within the vast game spaces, effectively simplifying the game without altering its fundamental nature. A specific example is used to illustrate the proposed method, and subsequent analysis includes findings on the structure and relationships between the resulting game subdivisions.

A primary advantage of using polarized muons to investigate new particles is the ease of identifying missing transverse energy by analyzing neutrino interactions where new particles might not be present. In these interactions, new particles could be hidden among efficiently produced vector bosons. We examine the potential for producing vector bosons through the weak interaction by converting virtual leptons into visible vector bosons. While this process is generally suppressed, the cross section increases significantly above a certain energy threshold, reaching up to 10 nb for charged muons with 1000 GeV of energy. By utilizing advanced detection methods, we can accurately identify the relevant particles and limit any new physics beyond the standard model. In addition to this, limiting other possible explanations for vector bosogenesis allows us to establish efficient upper cross section limits or even discover vector bosogenesis in future muon colliders.

The rapid advancement of AI models' capabilities has been hindered by a lack of autonomy in hardware and software aspects. This limitation has been exacerbated by the scale and complexity of contemporary reinforcement learning systems, which rely on massive models and operate across vast distributions of environments. Such settings necessitate simultaneous interactions from several agents and require coordination among a range of components, including researchers, engineers, and technicians. Consequently, there is a pressing need for these multi-component setups to be both highly modular and adaptable. This modularity would facilitate the translation of specialized knowledge into targeted advancements in specific components, rather than leading to costly and disruptive model overhauls. Although previous models have been sufficiently modular for small-scale applications, their large-scale counterparts have been found to be tightly interwoven models rather than truly modulated systems. Our investigation addresses this discrepancy by introducing a novel framework that separates critical functions into distinct, interchangeable modules, and we validate our approach through a large-scale model-driven reinforcement learning application, demonstrating that this framework enables critical operations, such as simulation-to-real transfer, to be executed by a single expert with technical expertise confined to one system component.

This article is a discussion of the foundational developments in formal logic that occurred at Chicago University during the years 1933 to 1935. The location was made significant for the advancement of formal logic due to the presence of J. Rosser, a young and dedicated assistant to A. Tarski, who worked in the department of mathematics at Chicago University. We explore the ideas of leading figures in formal logic, including Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and others, and discuss how they shaped the field. In addition, the article examines the technical aspects of axiomatized systems and the limitations they face, as well as the philosophical implications of these limitations. The discussion is contextualized by the historical events of the time, including the impact of World War II on the figures discussed.

This research builds upon the 'Three Spheres Theorem' in functions, extending it to eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator within Clifford Analysis. We reprove the original theorem from Faraut and Koranyi, then provide an adjusted proof that maintains the 'Clifford Analysis' context, and establish an generalization of the original result.

Reconstruction methods that consider uncertainty are crucial in the application of imaging technologies to areas like scientific imaging. Specifically, uncertainty maps indicating varying reliability of reconstructed images across different spatial and spectral dimensions are particularly useful. Our study focuses on a challenging inverse problem, the MEGa-CT, which aims to retrieve a CT image from partial and noisy spectral measurements. We introduce a new model, the Regularized Conditional Gan Uncertainty map, which is capable of generating accurate and diverse uncertainty maps that are tailored to specific measurements, adhere to a known physical constraint, and prevent reliability overestimation in unmeasured areas. We evaluate our network's effectiveness through the Cherenken task and a set of synthetic tests, comparing it to existing methods and highlighting its advancements.

This report delves into the findings of a study on fractional-order dynamical systems, specifically those with the Rouse-Traub manifold, as well as other periodic and quasi-periodic invariant sets. Utilizing numerical methods, evidence was found of complex dynamics, including break-downs of a torus with periodic behavior induced by a transcritical bifurcation of quasi-periodic orbits, as well as the generation of chaotic attractors through the interaction of saddle-type fixed points and periodic orbits of various orders. Furthermore, in a system representing a four-variable fractional-order lattice model, the study discovered the absence of invariant surfaces of the TC3 periodic orbit and the formation of chaotic behavior in an otherwise simple lattice model.

This study analyzes scintillation data from the bright pulsar, B1133+16, to investigate the interstellar environment in the galaxy's thin disk. A total of 1114542 pulses were obtained using the Parkes telescope over 11 observation sessions lasting 2.5 hours each between 2014 and 2015. The distribution of amplitude fluctuations was modeled using a stochastic process involving a family of stochastic operators applied to a log-normal distribution. Key parameters were determined through maximum likelihood estimation. The results revealed that the interstellar medium around the pulsar contains a significant population of dense solitons with radii approximately 0.4 parsecs and number densities of $10^4$ cm$^{-3}$, with an overall fraction of $10^{-5}$ relative to the local environment. These findings are compared to previous studies based on data from other pulsars observed with the Parkes telescope and the Nancay radio telescope.

A Deep Neural Network Generative Model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is introduced in this work. By leveraging the stable, source-filter structure found in human speech and singing, the model only predicts a short segment of a single quasi-periodic waveform instead of the entire sequence. A carefully designed pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network is what the model uses to represent the net output function over a single quasi-periodic period. Training the network to predict only the non-repeating part of the waveform significantly reduces data requirements, making models smaller and more efficient. A five-order QP-WaveNet is then trained on singing speech to demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, outperforming traditional models in quality assessments and achieving higher correlation with ground truth features like F0 and spectral centroid. When training on musical scores, QP-WaveNet also shows a 10x vocabulary size reduction, smaller model size, and faster sampling speed compared to existing models.

theory of 2-categories. Its importance is even more pronounced when considering
stable $\infty$-categories as part of an algebraic approach to higher category
theory. Nonetheless, a basic, intuitive explanation for this phenomenon has so
far been elusive. We address this gap by demonstrating that taking homological
perpendicular complements forms a shadow of an idomon in stably enriched 6-categories.

Determining the direction of sounds in our environment is primarily based on comparing the timing and intensity of sounds reaching each ear. Although this basic sound localization mechanism is well-established, there's no supporting evidence from empirical data, as experiments involving animals or humans have historically relied on artificial methods to vary interaural time and intensity. In contrast, natural sounds often differ in arrival times and intensities at each ear due to the physical properties of our heads. In this study, we investigate whether listeners can utilize these information sources to effectively localize sounds in space. Our findings indicate that humans are capable of utilizing even minute differences in interaural time and intensity variations, enabling us to localize sounds emanating from anywhere, including spaces in front of, to the sides, or behind us.

The success of graph neural networks in analyzing static graphs can be attributed in part to their ability to pool information from neighboring nodes. To achieve this, many GNN models have adopted Eulerian paths and tree-based structures as a pooling method. However, these approaches are limited when it comes to real-world graphs that contain directed edges with varying weights. As a result, these models may produce inaccurate results in such scenarios. In this work, we introduce a new type of graph neural network called Lorentzian GNN, which is based on a new mathematical structure known as a Fejer convex path. Our model ensures information conservation and utilizes convex combinations to pool information from the graph's nodes as a side benefit. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Lorentxian GNNs through a range of experiments, including link prediction, node classification, and semi-supervised node classification tasks. The results show that our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by significant margins.

A chemical engagement between two characters, depicted as van and airplane, drives our innovative design called the airboat plane. Taking the unique features of the airboat plane as input, reversing physics principles generates three distinct and unexpected designs for a functional aircraft.

We present a new statistical model that we call the exponential delay devaluation distribution, which extends the exponential delay distribution by incorporating the degree of long-tail heaviness as a key parameter. This new model is based on the Tsallis entropy and we investigate its fundamental properties, including the calculation of its entropy, moments, and reliability and hazard rates, as well as order statistics and its Bayesian estimation. We also examine the new model's nested structure, which allows us to derive submodels, and we compare it to other related distributions. We then use maximum likelihood estimation to estimate the model's parameters and assess its fit to datasets, which include the Gumbel distribution as a special case. We also propose the Bayesian estimation method for the model's parameters and present graphical representations of the estimated distributions and their hazard and reliability rates. We find that the new distribution offers a more flexible structure than its sibling distributions and can be used as a robust alternative in various fields of study.

In recent months, several gravitational wave detectors have identified anomalies that suggest the existence of new forms of gravity, characterized by their ability to propagate at exceptionally high speeds, up to 1.23 times the speed of light, with a margin of error of approximately five percent. This discovery has prompted theorists to explore potential modifications to general relativity, including a unique class of models known as harmonic gravity, first introduced in the 1950s. Despite previous claims that harmonic gravity leads to mathematical singularities when paired with first-order gravity theories, this paper argues that these strange outcomes are likely the result of difficult calculation methods and not inherent flaws in the harmonic gravity framework itself. This study translates canonical conditions from the Weyl-Wigner phase space representation to a more familiar form. Although previously established for convex cases, an explicit formulation for non-convex canonical conditions was not readily available. In this study, we derive these conditions directly from the phase space representation, which leads to an interesting interpretation of the density matrix as a weighted sum of shifted projection operators. This approach allows us to translate abstract canonical conditions into features of weighted and displaced operators, ultimately providing a novel perspective on the canonical ensembles of a single quantum particle. Notably, we illustrate this approach with detailed examples involving the harmonic oscillator and a localized particle in an infinite well.

Researchers have examined the implications of the "scoto-seesaw" dark sector model's simplest implementation, focusing on its parameters that determine the stability of the electroweak vacuum and its potential for explaining the CMS anomaly observed in muon magnetic dipole measurements. By analyzing a specific part of the dark sector's parameter space, predictions for dark matter observations made by the XENONnT experiment were derived, and the magnitude of the CMS anomaly in muon magnetic dipole measurements was found to be F84. Additionally, the dark sector's contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment of muons exceeds the required value by a factor of 1.6-2 in certain regions of its parameter space, which could be tested through searches for heavy Higgs boson decays at the LHC with expected sensitivities of 95%-99%. For WIMP dark matter, the mass of the particle is found to be 15-40 GeV with a verification of the scoto-seesaw dark sector model's predictions that can be made through XenonnT and LHC experiments, which are projected to cover 80%-95% of the model's parameter space relevant for the muon anomaly.

Blending of $t_{2g}$ orbitals with $e_g$ orbitals in transition metal compounds is typically hindered by symmetry, resulting in a unique pattern of crystal field splitting. However, in compounds with local $C_2$ symmetry, we observe interference of these orbitals without losing the characteristic $t_{2g}$ splitting characteristic. We investigated a range of local $C_2$ symmetric compounds made from Sc, Y, Ru, Ir and Bi, and found that the bond angles and distances between atoms play a crucial role in raising the bond-like $t_{2g}$ orbital above the anti-bonding $e_g$ orbital. This distinctive arrangement of orbital energies has a significant impact on the material properties of compounds containing Ru and Ir, and we were able to recreate these patterns through density functional theory calculations.

Rational symplectic transformations lead to relationships between relative quantum homology rings, denoted as $\mathrm{QH}_\star(M,\gamma)$ and $\mathrm{QH}_\star(M,\delta)$, where $e^\gamma$ and $e^\delta$ represent Thom classes of torsion bundles over a manifold $M$. These relationships are expressed through polynomial elements with respect to the q-variable and the middle insertion variable, specifically $\Phi_\alpha$ elements. Additionally, there are stability properties of these polynomial elements under certain conditions related to the degrees of the bundles. When the bundles in question are trivial, this research generalizes previous findings that extended the properties originally discovered by Fukuma, Hosomoto, and Kawai from closed to relative symplectic categories.

Overacting visualization techniques have been employed to distinguish experienced practitioners from ordinary individuals, with several methods being explored to differentiate trained nurses from untrained individuals. Despite various studies that successfully differentiated professionals from non-professionals in areas like medical imaging interpretation, nursing disciplines, and foreign language learning, an unaddressed challenge lies in differentiating licensed nurses from novices in illness management by modifying medical images. To tackle this problem, our research involves creating a new dataset consisting of 10,000 images modified with varying degrees of illness visualization, and then successfully testing our approach by using it to distinguish licensed nurses from novices in disease management with modified images, achieving a higher accuracy of 0.65 compared to 0.6 without this new dataset. To provide a practical and adaptable solution, we also offer an open-source illness-aware visual transformation method that can be applied to a wide range of diseases, thereby extending the applicability of our findings.

High-dimensionality is a common issue in many datasets, complicating their visualization and analysis due to the curse of dimensionality. Traditional graphical methods are effective for examining and understanding data, yet they struggle with high-dimensional sets. This study introduces an innovative approach to address the challenges posed by high dimensionality through the development of a new visualization tool called ViDaExpert. This instrument combines a linear projection technique known as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with a nonlinear method called Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) to create a comprehensive examination and visualization of data. ViDaExpert enables researchers to investigate the relationships between variables and observations in an examination map, while also allowing for the selection of specific dimensions to be analyzed non-linearly after the initial PCA projection. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of ViDaExpert through its successful application to a dataset comprising 18 dimensions and 429 observations, resulting in clear examination of the structure of a complex virologic time series.
